why: Holiday and summer liquidity and fund-manager behaviour make the Nov-Apr half of the year historically stronger; the sellers are summer-leavers who shift risk by calendar.
When the yield curve flattens sharply, banks lend less and slow-moving investors keep holding risk into the downturn; staying out of equities then avoids their losses.
Investors anchor on old prices and under-react to news, so markets that rose over the past year (skipping the last month) tend to keep rising; the sellers are anchored holders.
Slow institutions and loss-averse investors under-react to price trends and sell late; trend followers get paid for stepping aside in long falls.
Forced sellers and people who buy insurance at any price create short-term over-reaction when the VIX spikes; calmer buyers are paid for supplying cash.
Risk-limit rules force funds to sell when volatility rises, so calm periods in an uptrend are when those funds stay invested; the edge is being invested only when forced sellers are absent.
Money flows slowly between markets; the markets with the strongest recent returns keep attracting it, and the laggards' holders are late sellers.
Pension, super and salary money arrives around month-end and start; buyers who must invest on a schedule push prices up, and sellers who ignore the calendar sell cheaper.
Headline-driven sellers dump after a burst of bad world news; calmer buyers collect the over-reaction (this idea only exists from the news start date).
Short-term sellers over-react inside a rising market; liquidity providers who buy a sharp 3-day drop are paid for the risk, and the sellers pay the spread.
